item.title: Tia Kemp Turns 50 Cent’s $6M Lawsuit Into A Fundraiser Joke
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Tia Kemp used a mock $6 million fundraiser to ridicule 50 Cent's lawsuit over her posts about his teenage son, Sire Jackson.
item.content:encoded:
Tia Kemp turned 50 Cent‘s $6 million lawsuit into a fundraising joke, sharing a mock GoFundMe-style graphic with a goal matching his demand.

“I need Money by Monday,” Kemp wrote in the caption. The GoFundMe-style image was a joke rather than a real fundraising campaign.

She also mocked him for using lawyers after making jokes at other people’s expense. Among her targets was his 2015 bankruptcy, which followed a court loss to another woman with ties to Rick Ross.

The lawsuit concerns posts about 50’s teenage son, Sire Jackson. As AllHipHop previously reported, the rapper sued Kemp on behalf of the 14-year-old in federal court in Los Angeles on October 26.

His complaint sought at least $6 million. It accused Kemp of defamation, invasion of privacy and intentional infliction of emotional distress over her social media posts.

The lawyers said she made up a medical diagnosis for Sire and linked it to sexually degrading claims about his mother, Daphne Joy. They also alleged Kemp kept posting after receiving a cease-and-desist letter.

Kemp’s bankruptcy jab reached back to Lastonia Leviston’s privacy case against 50. Leviston, who shares a daughter with Ross, sued over a sex video the rapper circulated while taunting him.

Jurors awarded her $5 million before 50 filed for bankruptcy on July 13, 2015. They later added $2 million in punitive damages. A subsequent bankruptcy agreement set her claim at $6 million.

The current fight also grew out of an incident involving Kemp’s adult son with Ross, William Roberts III. He told police a man threatened him with a gun and struck him in the head in Daytona Beach on October 11.

50 mocked William for calling police and offered help for the accused attacker.

Separately, a Florida judge granted a temporary injunction requiring Kemp to stay at least 500 feet from Sire and barring direct or indirect contact, including through social media.

That order expires November 3, when both sides are scheduled to appear in court for a hearing on a possible longer injunction.

item.title: Jose Bodega Pleads The Fifth In Yella Beezy’s MO3 Murder Trial
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Jose Bodega invoked the Fifth Amendment outside the jury's presence when questioned in Yella Beezy's MO3 murder trial.
item.content:encoded:
Jose Bodega took the stand in Yella Beezy‘s MO3 murder trial Thursday (October 29), but he would not repeat the account he had given a grand jury.

With the jury out of the Dallas courtroom, the rapper repeatedly invoked the Fifth Amendment when asked about his past statements. He also declined to answer a defense question about an alleged recantation.

The exchange put the focus on a witness who had previously agreed to help prosecutors. Bodega, whose legal name is Theodore Thomas, is Yella Beezy’s childhood friend. His cooperation agreement came through a separate federal drug case.

Yella Beezy, legally named Markies Conway, pleaded not guilty to capital murder and denied hiring Kewon White to kill MO3. The state accused him of arranging the fatal attack on his fellow Dallas rapper.

Bodega did answer some early questions. He confirmed that he appeared before a Dallas County grand jury on February 13, 2025. A prosecutor then showed him a record containing 143 pages of testimony and asked him to revisit what he had said.

That was where the answers largely stopped. Questions about prior accounts involving White and other people in the case drew repeated Fifth Amendment responses, as shown in WFAA’s courtroom footage.

The prosecutor asked about Get Rich Cartel, a feud involving the rappers and Bodega’s whereabouts in California around the time of MO3’s death. He also asked about a conversation at a barbershop. Bodega declined to discuss those subjects rather than confirm the details laid out in the questions.

Judge Chika Anyiam noted that Bodega was invoking the Fifth on all material questions and asked the state how it wanted to proceed. When the defense got its turn, an attorney asked whether Bodega had recanted to a detective with a lawyer present. Bodega invoked the Fifth again.

His earlier cooperation had already come under scrutiny. At an October 6 hearing, defense expert Julianna Moore testified that Bodega pleaded guilty to drug conspiracy and agreed to assist in the murder case. She also said a gun charge against him had been dismissed.

MO3, whose legal name was Melvin Noble, was killed on November 11, 2020. White chased him on foot along Interstate 35E and shot him with a rifle. In White’s separate case, a jury convicted him of capital murder and he received life without parole, according to the Dallas County district attorney’s office.

After Bodega stepped down Thursday, Judge Anyiam directed his attorney to keep him in the courthouse in case he was called back to the stand.

item.title: Byron Allen Cashes Out Entire Starz Stake With Nearly $20M Gain
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Byron Allen sold his entire Starz stake for about $44.9 million after paying $25 million for the shares earlier this year.
item.content:encoded:
Byron Allen sold his entire Starz stake for about $44.9 million, turning a $25 million bet on the home of “Power” into a gain of nearly $20 million.

The exit surfaced in an October 29 securities disclosure, according to Variety. Allen sold the roughly 1.8 million shares he held during August and September, months after buying into the pay-TV and streaming company.

His Beverly Hills-based investment firm, Allen Family Capital, made the sales in several batches. Deadline reported that prices ranged from about $21 to $27 per share.

That closed out an investment that had raised a much bigger question: Would Allen try to buy Starz outright?

In March, he bought a 10.7 percent stake from former Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin’s Liberty 77 investment funds. The purchase covered 1,803,786 shares at $13.86 each, TheWrap reported. Before that deal, Allen had no Starz shares under his ownership or control.

His firm left room for several paths when it announced the purchase. It could buy more stock or sell its holdings as it weighed Starz’s business and market conditions. The firm also said it could discuss strategy with the company’s board and management.

Allen’s ambitions soon went beyond holding shares. Starz adopted a “poison pill” after his investment, a defense meant to make an unwanted takeover harder. The Hollywood Reporter reported that Allen still wanted control of the company despite that move.

He repeated that goal in a “Rapid Response” interview published July 31. Speaking with host Bob Safian, Allen laid out plans to build up Starz’s comedy offerings and pursue sports rights if he gained control.

“I can save Starz. Starz needs to be saved,” Allen said in that earlier interview.

For Hip-Hop viewers, the company was already familiar territory.

AllHipHop covered Allen’s March investment against the backdrop of 50 Cent’s television business there. The rapper-producer helped build the “Power” franchise at Starz, which also carried “BMF.”

Starz separated from Lionsgate in 2025. The company reported its latest quarterly results Thursday, alongside news of Allen’s exit. Its net loss fell to $34.8 million from $52.6 million a year earlier, while streaming revenue rose 1.7 percent to $226.6 million.

item.title: Lil Yachty Joins Kilby Block Party 2027 Headliners
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Lil Yachty joined the Kilby Block Party 2027 headliners, with the three-day Utah festival set for May 14-16 in Salt Lake City.
item.content:encoded:
Lil Yachty was named one of six headliners for Kilby Block Party 2027, putting him on the bill for the Utah festival’s May 14-16 return.

The lineup announced October 28 also includes Deftones, Fontaines D.C., The Strokes, Slayyyter and Jungle at the top. The three-day event will take place at Utah State Fairpark in Salt Lake City.

Three-day general admission passes cost $245, while VIP passes cost $409, according to Deseret News. They go on sale October 29 at 10 a.m. MDT, or noon EDT. Early bird passes have sold out.

Yachty has spent years making music beyond the sound that first brought him to rap fans. His 2023 album Let’s Start Here took a turn into psychedelic rock, a direction he had teased in 2022 when he described the planned project as a non-rap album.

That shift also led him to explain what he wanted from his career. At a January 2023 listening event, he said he wanted people to take him seriously as an artist. Some listeners heard that as a slight against rap.

In a Rap Radar interview covered by AllHipHop that February, he said the point was that he did more than rap. He recalled making Michigan Boy Boat and doing freestyles while trying to prove himself as a rapper.

“That’s when I was trying to prove I’m a rapper. But I’m past that. Now, I’m proving I’m an artist,” he said.

Let’s Start Here also gave him a new set of chart milestones. The album entered at No. 1 on Billboard’s Top Rock Albums, Top Alternative Albums and Top Rock & Alternative Albums charts. It was his first album to lead any Billboard album chart.

Across all genres, the project debuted at No. 9 on the Billboard 200 with 36,000 equivalent album units in its first week. That made it his third Top 10 album.

Kilby has grown since its 2019 start as a block party at Kilby Court, later moving to the fairpark. The 2027 lineup also includes Utah acts Olympic Deth and Choir Boy. More artists remain unannounced, and organizers have yet to announce when single-day passes will be available.

item.title: Becky G Mourns Dolores Huerta With Personal Tribute
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Becky G mourned Dolores Huerta with a personal tribute after the labor leader and civil rights activist died at 96.
item.content:encoded:
Becky G mourned Dolores Huerta on October 28, sharing a personal farewell after the labor leader died at 96.

The singer posted a black-and-white photo of Huerta on Instagram Stories, according to Rolling Stone.

“Dolores, knowing you is one of my life’s greatest joys and inspirations,” Becky wrote, the outlet reported. Her message also recalled their shared laughs and dances.

The two had appeared together at La Cena’s celebration of Latino culture at NeueHouse Hollywood on February 21, 2025. Photographer Presley Ann documented the pair at the event for Getty Images. Huerta received La Cena’s Luminary Award during that year’s celebration.

This April, Becky also joined Karol G’s Coachella set, where the headliner spoke about the Latino community and immigration enforcement.

Huerta died at home in Bakersfield, California, with close family around her, her foundation said. Her family asked for privacy and said plans to honor her life would follow.

The organizer had spent decades fighting for people who grew and picked the nation’s food. She co-founded the National Farm Workers Association with Cesar Chavez in 1962. It later joined with the Filipino-led Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee to form the union that became the United Farm Workers.

Her work reached shoppers as well as people in the fields. During the grape boycott, Huerta led the campaign on the East Coast. She moved to New York and worked to get small stores on board before taking the fight to big grocery chains, according to the National Park Service.

At the bargaining table, she helped secure better pay and working conditions. Her push for change also reached state lawmakers. She helped win California’s 1975 Agricultural Labor Relations Act, which gave farmworkers the right to organize and bargain as a group.

The Dolores Huerta Foundation carried that community work forward. Its programs helped residents organize around schools, clean air and water and other local needs. In 2012, President Barack Obama awarded Huerta the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

The foundation plans to open the Dolores Huerta Peace and Justice Cultural Center in the Central Valley in 2027. In place of flowers or gifts, Huerta requested contributions to the foundation.

item.title: Suno Targets Apple’s AI Deals
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Suno challenged Apple's effort to block testimony, arguing that private music deals could support its AI copyright defense.
item.content:encoded:
Suno fought Apple’s bid to block testimony on October 27, tying four narrowed topics to its fair use and copyright misuse defenses, Digital Music News reported.

The questions covered label licensing and AI talks, Apple’s prospects without major catalogs, streaming fraud and communications about the case, including label agents.

Suno accused Universal Music Group and Sony Music of using their catalogs to win AI restrictions. Its filing targeted “negotiations to restrict Apple’s ability to offer AI-generated content,” according to the report. The company also pointed to guaranteed royalties and rules keeping AI tracks outside royalty pools.

Apple had already pushed back on how much of its business Suno could examine. As AllHipHop reported, Apple argued that the demand reached private commercial information and that the labels themselves could provide relevant evidence. Its position was that it had supplied data about AI music on the service.

Fair use turns in part on what a use does to the market for a copyrighted work and what that work is worth. That is one of four factors in federal copyright law. The others concern why and how the work was used, what kind of work it is and how much was taken, including the importance of that portion. The law also calls for weighing whether the use serves a commercial purpose or nonprofit education.

The labels’ broader case accused Suno of using their recordings to train its tools without permission. They also argued that the resulting AI tracks competed with those recordings. Suno claimed fair use. For rappers, singers and producers, the stakes include the streams their recordings draw and the money tied to that listening. Warner Music Group, which initially joined the lawsuit, settled with Suno in 2025.

A separate lawsuit showed how closely that fight touched rap production. Music publisher Reservoir accused Suno of generating tracks with producer tags, the brief audio signatures that identify beatmakers. The publisher sought $157.5 million over 1,050 works, AllHipHop previously reported. That case was separate from the Universal and Sony lawsuit behind Apple’s testimony dispute.

Apple’s request to cancel the testimony demand or protect its information was listed for December 1.

item.title: Kim Kardashian Held At Gunpoint In Uganda, Producer Claims In Biography
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Kim Kardashian allegedly faced a gun on a Uganda trip with Kanye West, according to a producer's biography account.
item.content:encoded:
Kim Kardashian had a police officer’s gun held to her head during a 2018 trip to Uganda with Kanye West, producer Farnaz Farjam alleged in Jonathan Van Meter’s new biography, “Citizen Kim.”

According to PEOPLE’s account of the book, Farjam said West feared being drugged and police searched rooms. She said she got her crew out on a private jet.

Viking released “Citizen Kim” on October 27. Van Meter, Vibe’s founding editor, told Forbes he spent five years working on the biography after a 2019 profile of Kardashian led him to propose a book about her.

The book drew on visits to her home, time on photo shoots and interviews with people from across her life. Van Meter told The Hollywood Reporter that she could review his manuscript for factual errors. He said she did not bar him from speaking to anyone or place topics off limits.

The couple’s Uganda visit included a meeting with President Yoweri Museveni at State House in Entebbe on October 15, 2018. His office described talks about tourism and investment. They gave Museveni a pair of white sneakers. West also pledged to build a tourism school, according to the president’s office.

The Uganda trip came two years after Kardashian survived an armed robbery in Paris, an attack that changed how she handled her security and public exposure.

In March 2017, AllHipHop reported that she cried on “Keeping Up With The Kardashians” over claims that the Paris robbery had been staged. She described the coverage as “really traumatizing.”

In the 2016 robbery, men posing as police forced their way into her Paris lodging, tied her up and took roughly $6 million in jewelry. Kardashian later told a French court that she thought she would die. A Paris court convicted eight defendants and acquitted two in May 2025.

“I learned to be more private,” Kardashian later said. “It’s not worth the risk.” The Associated Press reported that she stopped sharing her location in real time and increased her security.

Van Meter did not interview West for “Citizen Kim.” He told The Hollywood Reporter he had concerns about whether it would be ethical to do so given West’s mental health.

item.title: Usher & Chris Brown Make Touring Chart History With $77.4 Million Month
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Usher and Chris Brown became the first co-headliners to lead Billboard's monthly touring chart with a $77.4 million September.
item.content:encoded:
Usher and Chris Brown made touring chart history together, becoming the first co-headliners to reach No. 1 on Billboard’s monthly Top Tours ranking.

“The R&B Tour” earned $77.4 million from 423,000 tickets across 10 September shows, according to Billboard Boxscore.

By the October 3 show in El Paso, Texas, their first 36 concerts had grossed $284.7 million and sold more than 1.5 million tickets. That already passed the $183.9 million earned by Usher’s “Past Present Future” tour.

The win gave Usher his first No. 1 on that chart. Brown previously led it for three straight months, from July through September 2025.

This time, the pair reached the top with less money than they made earlier in the summer. July brought in $98.4 million and August added $91.8 million. Both months put them at No. 3, behind BTS and The Weeknd.

For Usher, the stadium partnership carried a point beyond his own career. Before the opening show, he told The Associated Press that R&B deserved the same large stages as other genres.

“It’s not about me and my brother coming together,” he said. “We come together in support of our fans of R&B.”

He also described the pairing as a long-held goal that stretched back to his role supporting Brown early in the younger singer’s career.

In a separate April interview, AP asked Usher about the upcoming tour with Brown. That pre-tour clip appears below.

Live Nation announced the joint stadium run in April, after the artists teased it together on Instagram. The first schedule listed 33 dates across the United States and Canada. The tour opened June 26 at Denver’s Empower Field at Mile High.

The promoter also announced a partnership with Global Citizen, pledging $1 from each ticket sold to the FIFA Global Citizen Education Fund. That commitment was intended to help children gain access to education around the world.

The show itself brought the two catalogs into one production. As AllHipHop previously reported, the singers traded sections across nine acts rather than each taking a separate full set. Mario, Eric Bellinger and Tank joined the production as backing vocalists who also performed their own hits.

The reported total remained incomplete: Billboard said four October shows had not yet been reported when it compiled the figures.

item.title: Catch Concert Venue Enters Lockdown After Double Shooting Leaves Two Men Wounded
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Catch's London show faces a venue lockdown as police investigate nearby gunfire that wounds two men, leaving one with lasting injuries.
item.content:encoded:
Catch’s London concert venue went into lockdown after a nearby double shooting left two men hospitalized and one with life-changing injuries.

The South London rapper performed at O2 Academy Islington on Tuesday night as police responded to gunfire near the Angel Central shopping complex. Officers received the call at 10:25 p.m. on October 27 and found two wounded men aged 33 and 27.

Police did not consider either man’s wounds life-threatening but described the older man’s injuries as life-changing, according to The Standard’s account of the investigation. The force had announced no arrests in its latest available account and was still trying to establish what happened.

The Nightly reported that the shooting prompted a lockdown at the concert venue during Catch’s concert. The police account did not identify Catch as a target or link either wounded man to her show.

Chief Superintendent Jason Stewart, who oversees local policing, urged people with information about the attack to help officers identify those involved.

“Violence has no place in our communities, and we are pursuing every available line of enquiry to identify those involved,” Stewart said.

Live Nation listed a 9 p.m. start for her October 27 show, with doors opening two hours before the performance.

The London booking came during a year that brought Catch a Best Hip-Hop Act nomination at the MOBO Awards. Her fellow nominees included Little Simz, Central Cee, Aitch and Loyle Carner at the 30th anniversary ceremony hosted by Eve and Eddie Kadi.

Catch had also worked with Dave on “Heisenberg” after a conversation on Instagram led to time together in the studio.

“From there it was just about energy and understanding. Once we worked together, it made sense straight away,” she told Notion about their creative partnership.

Back in Islington, police put tape across part of Liverpool Road and the approach to Angel Central as they examined the scene. Stewart said extra officers would patrol the area over the following days while police worked with partners to reopen the shopping complex.

item.title: Mello Buckzz Reportedly Gets Two-Year Prison Term In Amari Blaze Case
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Mello Buckzz reportedly received two years in prison after a probation violation in the battery case involving Amari Blaze.
item.content:encoded:
Mello Buckzz reportedly received a two-year prison sentence on October 22 after admitting she violated probation in the battery case involving fellow Chicago rapper Amari Blaze.

Judge Patrick K. Coughlin resentenced the rapper, whose legal name is Melanie U. Doyle, in Cook County, according to a published account of the court records. The report said she received 197 days of credit for time already served. Her sentence also included six months of mandatory supervised release after prison.

She was first sentenced to probation. The Chicago Sun-Times reported that Mello pleaded guilty on April 17, 2025, received 30 months of probation and was ordered to stay away from Amari.

The two had once shared a record, not a court case. Amari appeared with Kashh Mir and Moni da G on “Mouskatool.” Mello also gained national attention through her Latto collaboration, “Boom Pt. 2.”

Their October 2023 clash in Calumet Park led to felony charges of aggravated battery causing great bodily harm and aggravated battery in a public place. The Sun-Times reported that court filings accused Mello of punching Amari in the face and causing her to fall through a window. The reported injuries included a broken nose and a hand wound that required tendon surgery. Her attorney, Edward L. Speights, had argued that she acted in self-defense.

A separate June 15 arrest brought a gun charge. ABC7 Chicago’s report below covered that earlier traffic stop, not the October sentencing.

Police stopped her Mercedes over an allegedly illegal windshield tint. Officers said they found a gun beneath the driver’s seat, suspected marijuana in her purse and an open bottle of alcohol inside the vehicle.

ABC7 reported that prosecutors accused her of lacking a valid Firearm Owner’s Identification card. She was charged with a felony weapons offense and two misdemeanor counts of resisting or obstructing an officer, along with traffic-related citations.

The sentencing report referenced an October 26 entry in the gun case indicating a sentence would run alongside the battery sentence. It did not establish the gun case’s full outcome or identify the conduct behind the probation violation.

An exact release date was not established in that report.
